To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

people often overestimate how much different values of an important attribute will affect their experienced happiness, and that they do so because they use their joint evaluation preferences when making predictions or choices for single evaluation events.

when people in JE make affective predictions or choices for SE, they often use their JE preferences rather their SE preferences, and that the difference that different attribute values make to happiness can be overpredicted.

people overpredict the effect of a change in a given attribute of an experience on their happiness, and this overprediction is caused by the fact that the utility of that attribute varies across JE and SE.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the difference between affective forecasts and affective experience.
the question of whether people can accurately predict their affective experience and whether they choose in an optimal way.
the distinction between the affective utility that people experience in the single evaluation mode and the affective utility people predict they will experience in the joint evaluation mode.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the distinction bias occurs when people in JE evaluate an attribute of an event to be experienced in the SE mode, and the utility function of the attribute varies between SE and JE.

the distinction bias occurs when people make predictions or choose in JE, when they will experience the event in SE, when their SE utility function for an attribute has a positive slope, and when their SE utility for the attribute is relatively low.
the distinction bias occurs whenever people are in JE mode and are making predictions or choices for an SE experience.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that people often make predictions and choices in the joint evaluation mode, which can result in systematic errors.
the distinction bias is the tendency to overpredict the difference an attribute (e. g., salary) will make to one's happiness when the difference between the attribute values is large.

people often fail to predict their future happiness and make poor choices because of their tendency to overpredict the difference in happiness that will be made by different values of an outcome attribute.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people often make inaccurate predictions and suboptimal choices due to their tendency to rely on JE preferences rather than SE preferences.
people's predictions and choices are often biased by the fact that people often experience events in the SE mode but often make predictions and choices in the JE mode.

people's affective predictions and choices are often distorted by the fact that they are not in the mode in which they are going to experience the event. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2020 APA, all rights reserved)
